text "Member"
[ax-20000030] button "Issue body actions"
heading "General proposal"
paragraph "protected modifier acts the same as private in terms of code generation and assignability, except that it is possible to access a protected member in any subclass of a class which declared the member."
heading "Examples"
code "class Base { protected myMember; } class Derived extends Base { foo() { return this.myMember; } // OK } var x = new Derived(); console.log(x.myMember); // Error, cannot access class Derived2 extends B"
[ax-20000031] button "Copy code to clipboard"
heading "Open Questions"
paragraph "After the last design meeting, the following open questions remained:"
heading "Is 'sibling' property access allowed?"
paragraph "C# and other IL languages prohibit this pattern, but Java allows it:"
code "class Base { protected x: string; } class Derived extends Base { foo(n: Base) { // Not allowed: cannot reference protected member through base class reference console.log(n.x); } }"
[ax-20000032] button "Copy code to clipboard"
paragraph "See these links for reasoning http://blogs.msdn.com/b/ericlippert/archive/2008/03/28/why-can-t-i-access-a-protected-member-from-a-derived-class-part-two-why-can-i.aspx http://stackoverflow.com/questio"
[ax-20000033] link "http://blogs.msdn.com/b/ericlippert/archive/2008/03/28/why-can-t-i-access-a-protected-member-from-a-derived-class-part-two-why-can-i.aspx"
[ax-20000034] link "http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1904782/whats-the-real-reason-for-preventing-protected-member-access"
heading "Are protected members subject to the \"same-declaration\" rule as private members for assignability/subtyping?"
paragraph "private members are considered equivalent for the purposes of assignability and subtyping if they are from the \"same declaration\". This isn't quite the rule you would want for protected members. Consi"
code "class Widget { protected inspector: WidgetInspector; } class SquareWidget extends Widget { // Use a more-specific 'inspector' protected inspector: SquareWidgetInspector; } class CircleWidget extends W"
[ax-20000035] button "Copy code to clipboard"
paragraph "If we took the verbatim \"same declaration\" rule from private, this assignment would be disallowed because w.inspector and c.inspector come from different declarations. It's not reasonable to have this"
paragraph "However, if we do not use the \"same declaration\" rule, then a SquareWidget would be assignable to a CirceWidget even if they both removed their extends clauses. This is not surprising if you're used t"
paragraph "A proposed rule was that we could have a notion of a \"parent\" declaration when a derived class's property overrides a base class property. This seems tractable for classes, but interfaces can extend m"
code "interface WatWidget1 extends Widget, CircleWidget { } interface WatWidget2 extends Widget, SquareWidget { } var ww1: WatWidget1; var ww2: WatWidget2; ww1 = new Widget(); // Allowed or not? ww1 = new C"
[ax-20000036] button "Copy code to clipboard"
heading "Can public properties be assigned to protected fields?"
code "class Point1 { x: number } var p1: Point1 = { x: 3 }; // Allowed class Point2 { private x: number } var p2: Point2 = { x: 3 }; // Disallowed class Point3 { protected x: number } var p: Point3 = { x: 3"
[ax-20000037] button "Copy code to clipboard"
paragraph "This is sort of a yes-or-no thing tangentially related to the previous question."

heading "General proposal"
paragraph "protected modifier acts the same as private in terms of code generation and assignability, except that it is possible to access a protected member in any subclass of a class which declared the member."
heading "Examples"
code "class Base { protected myMember; } class Derived extends Base { foo() { return this.myMember; } // OK } var x = new Derived(); console.log(x.myMember); // Error, cannot access class Derived2 extends B"

heading "Open Questions"
paragraph "After the last design meeting, the following open questions remained:"
heading "Is 'sibling' property access allowed?"
paragraph "C# and other IL languages prohibit this pattern, but Java allows it:"
code "class Base { protected x: string; } class Derived extends Base { foo(n: Base) { // Not allowed: cannot reference protected member through base class reference console.log(n.x); } }"

heading "Are protected members subject to the \"same-declaration\" rule as private members for assignability/subtyping?"
paragraph "private members are considered equivalent for the purposes of assignability and subtyping if they are from the \"same declaration\". This isn't quite the rule you would want for protected members. Consi"
code "class Widget { protected inspector: WidgetInspector; } class SquareWidget extends Widget { // Use a more-specific 'inspector' protected inspector: SquareWidgetInspector; } class CircleWidget extends W"
